Zap history at zapier.com/app/history, exported as JSON
None by default; each run is fresh (a Sheet row can act as memory)

questions.explanation: The Zap is the simplest night-shift worker: one alarm clock and one job. It cannot choose, which is why it is cheap and easy to check.
questions.trap: Memory is the weakest part of a Zap; students often claim the Zap 'remembers' last run.
questions.source: PS5 brief read with Week 6's five parts

questions.stem: A classmate's stock-watch Zap kept saying Success in Zap history while the email body was all #N/A. What does this teach about records, and how would you place the agent on the Week 7 map?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Success' in Zap history means the run completed, which is Week 6's 'green means the machines held, not that the job was done'; the job, a readable briefing, still failed. Only reading the output against the record and against a source such as Google Finance shows that, and the fix (an IFERROR-style formula) had to be predicted and re-tested on the same tricky case. On the Week 7 map the prices have a right answer, but the Buy/Sell/Hold line has no single right answer, and the agent prepares the briefing alone while the person could decide alone. So it sits in 'A person decides, AI alongside' (bottom right): the analyst checks one price against Google Finance each morning before making the trading decision. A plain summary with no recommendation would move one box left, to 'AI alone, with checks'.
questions.explanation: (1) the Week 6 sentence quoted and applied (a successful run can still be wrong); (2) the difference between the output and the record; (3) the two map questions answered with evidence from the runs; (4) who/what/when for the person; (5) the 'what would move it' line.
questions.source: PS5 stock-watch guide; Week 6 'Green means the machines held'

questions.stem: A classmate's PS5 (automate a task with a Zapier agent) Zap emails customers a weekly summary. They wrote the five-line agent card after the three runs, and line 4 says 'It must never: send anything rude — the prompt says be polite'. What is wrong, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: The agent card must be written before the first run, time-stamped in its header, so it records what you expected before you saw the output — the same falsificationist habit as predictions.md in PS4 (heuristic evaluation); written afterwards, it is only a description. Line 4, 'It must never', needs one thing and the setting that stops it, and 'the prompt says be polite' is a sentence, not a setting. A better line is 'It must never send to a customer — the Gmail step is Create Draft, not Send Email', so a person reads and sends each draft. The proof that the Zap ran as its card says is Zap history, Zapier's own record of every run, matched to each output, because an email arriving shows only the output, not the run. Remember too that 'green means the machines held, not that the job was done', so each of the three runs must be checked against the record.
questions.explanation: (1) timing of the card (before the first run) and why; (2) line 4 needs a setting, not a sentence; (3) a concrete enforcing setting (Create Draft); (4) Zap history as the record vs the output; (5) checking each run.
questions.source: PS5 brief, Step 1 and the five-line agent card; Week 6 'Green means the machines held'

questions.stem: In the Banking CRM Onboarding Agent built by Group 4 (Week 8 session), Gmail sends only after the CRM Manager clicks Approve in a 'Human in the Loop' step. What makes it top-right ('Agents run it, a person judges') rather than bottom-right ('A person decides, AI alongside')?
options: A human is accountable for the email that goes out
The process pauses for the person's judgment, then continues
Gemini wrote three campaign options for the manager to compare
The manager is a senior person with signing authority over campaigns
questions.explanation: 'Judgment by a person, or accountability, does not on its own make it top-right.' Top-right needs two things: no single right answer, and a process that pauses for the person's judgment and then continues with it. The Zap stops at Request Approval and Gmail sends only afterwards, so the manager's judgment sits inside the run.
questions.trap: 'A human is accountable' is explicitly rejected in the deck: accountability does not place a task. Gemini drafting options and the manager's seniority do not place it either.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, CRM placement reasoning

questions.stem: In Group 4's Expense Claim Pre-Check agent (Week 8 session), Zap history showed 'Successful' for every run, yet some emails said a 67-day-late claim was 'OK'. What was the cause and the lesson?
options: Gemini hallucinated the dates; a bigger model would fix it
The manager approved the late claim by mistake in the sheet
Zapier's free plan dropped the date-check step on some of the runs without warning
An empty column shifted every field; 'a run can succeed and still be wrong'
questions.explanation: 'Successful runs, wrong emails': an empty column shifted every check, so a 67-day-late taxi claim said 'OK'. 'A run can succeed and still be wrong. Zap history said Successful every time.' Caught only by comparing each email against its sheet row.
questions.trap: 'Gemini hallucinated the dates' is the 'smarter model' trap; no model was involved in the shifted column. The free plan did not drop steps either.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, Expense failure → fix → retest

questions.stem: In Group 4's Banking CRM Onboarding Agent (Week 8 session), customer BANK_012 had already deposited. Gemini correctly returned NO_CAMPAIGN, but the Zap still asked the manager to approve. Group 4 (the Week 8 Zapier-agents team) called this:
options: An AI error, fixed by rewriting the Gemini prompt
A hallucination by Gemini, fixed by switching to a bigger, newer model
'A workflow-control fault, not an AI error', fixed with a Filter
A consent bug in the form, fixed by a new checkbox
questions.explanation: The model was right; the flowchart was wrong. Fix: a Filter by Zapier step before approval that continues only if SEND_FOR_APPROVAL. This separates the model from the harness, as Week 5 taught.
questions.trap: Blaming the AI when the flowchart failed is the trap.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, CRM failure → fix

questions.stem: Why is Group 4's MBairline Feedback Assistant (Week 8 session) placed bottom-right, 'A person decides, AI alongside', even though the manager reviews every report?
options: Because the manager is accountable for service recovery outcomes
Because passenger feedback has a right answer the agent can find
Because the Gmail step is Create Draft, so nothing is sent alone
'the agent's outputs are complete without the person, and the person decides independently'
questions.explanation: 'Human accountability is not what places it here. What matters is that the agent's outputs are complete without the person, and the person decides independently.' Feedback has no single right answer (Map question 1 (Is there a right answer?) = no), and either party could do the work alone (Map question 2 (Must people and AI work together?) = no): the manager 'could do all of it manually'; using both is faster, not required.
questions.trap: 'The Gmail step is Create Draft' is the 'never' setting, not the placement reason. 'Feedback has a right answer' is false (an apology, an investigation or a call could each be right). 'The manager is accountable' is the reason the deck rejects.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, MBairline placement reasoning

questions.stem: In Group 4's Zapier agents (Week 8 session), which 'never' rule is enforced by a setting rather than by a prompt?
options: 'Never email staff' — the AI is told to be careful with mail
'Never approve a claim' — the prompt says please do not
'Never send a customer reply' — the Gmail step is Create Draft
'Never target a depositor' — a comment in the sheet says so
questions.explanation: A setting is something the harness enforces; a prompt 'can only ask' (Week 9's rule for Q3 — What can it touch?). Create Draft instead of Send Email removes the sending action from the Zap entirely, so no sentence anywhere can make it send.
questions.trap: The other three are all sentences the model reads or a comment a person reads; none of them removes the action.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, agent cards; Week 9 slide 10

questions.stem: Week 9 opened with a recap of what each week added to an agent. What did Week 8 add?
options: Planning and evaluation of each agent's output
Memory between runs, and hands: tools, MCP connectors and skills
The brain, and the loop that picks each next step until a stop rule
Trust, governance and the capstone project
questions.explanation: The recap: Week 7 gave the brain — a model choosing each next step in a loop. 'Week 8: memory kept between runs, and hands made of tools, MCP connectors and skills.' The Week 7 and 8 studios also added 'a clock that starts a run and a person at the gate' (drafts and pull requests). Memory hook: Week 7 = brain and loop; Week 8 = memory and hands; Week 9 = reading and placing products.
questions.trap: 'The brain and the loop' is Week 7. 'Planning and evaluation' and 'trust and governance' are later topics (Weeks 9–10).
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 3 'Where we are'

questions.stem: Match each agent built by Group 4 (who led the Week 8 session on four Zapier agents) to its Week 7 map quadrant and the person's role.

pairs.right: A person leads, AI inside — the line manager signs off what the agent checked
Agents run it, a person judges — the CRM Manager approves inside the run, before Gmail
AI alone, with checks — HR spot-checks one day's numbers every Friday
A person decides, AI alongside — the manager decides independently using the draft

questions.explanation: Each agent answers the two map questions differently — Map question 1 (Is there a right answer?), Map question 2 (Must people and AI work together?): Expense yes/yes, CRM no/yes, Manpower yes/no, MBairline no/no. The person also sits in a different place: the last step (Expense), inside the run before Gmail (CRM), outside on Friday (Manpower), after the run, owning the case (MBairline).
questions.trap: CRM vs MBairline both have a manager review; only CRM's process pauses and continues with the judgment.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, four agents table

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacy wants an agent that reads each prescription, checks dose limits and drug interactions against a rulebook, and emails a flag to the pharmacist, who signs off. Place it on the Week 7 map, name the person's role, and say what change would move it and where.
questions.modelAnswer: Map question 1 (Is there a right answer?): yes — dose limits and interaction rules are fixed, so 'the same claim always gets the same result'. Map question 2 (Must people and AI work together?): yes — a named pharmacist must approve, and the agent cannot see the patient. So it sits in 'A person leads, AI inside' (top left): the pharmacist signs off what the agent has checked on every prescription, within a set time, and a FAIL is a flag, not a rejection. If low-risk repeat prescriptions that pass were dispensed automatically with a weekly sample audit, the second question would flip to 'either can do it alone' and the task would move to 'AI alone, with checks'. The 'never dispense' rule should be a setting — the only action in the Zap is an email to the pharmacist, with no dispensing action at all — not prompt wording.
questions.explanation: (1) both map questions answered with a reason; (2) the exact title; (3) who/what/when for the pharmacist; (4) the move, with which question flips and where it lands; (5) the 'never' enforced by a setting, not a prompt.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session applied to a new domain

questions.stem: Match each move proposed by Group 4 (who led the Week 8 session on four Zapier agents) to the map question that flips and where the agent lands.

pairs.left: Expense Claim Pre-Check: claims under S$20 that pass are approved automatically; finance audits monthly
pairs.right: Map question 2 (Must people and AI work together?) yes → no; lands in 'AI alone, with checks'

pairs.left: Banking CRM Onboarding Agent: the agent only suggests campaigns; the manager writes and sends
pairs.right: Map question 2 (Must people and AI work together?) yes → no; lands in 'A person decides, AI alongside'

pairs.left: Daily Manpower Report: on high-absence days it recommends staff moves for the head to weigh
pairs.right: Map question 1 (Is there a right answer?) yes → no; lands in 'A person decides, AI alongside'

pairs.left: MBairline Feedback Assistant: the agent coordinates follow-up; manager judgments steer the process
pairs.right: Map question 2 (Must people and AI work together?) no → yes; lands in 'Agents run it, a person judges'

questions.explanation: 'Only Question 1 (Is there a right answer?) moves the HR agent; the other three change Question 2 (Must people and AI work together?). Removing an approval does not by itself move an agent: the work has to change.' Tip: for each move, ask which of the two map questions now has a different answer; exactly one flips each time.
questions.trap: A change that flips neither question (a different sending time, a second email address, a weekly audit added to the same work) moves nothing.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, 'What would move each agent?'

questions.stem: A manager says, 'Our agent has a human approval step, so it must be top-right (Agents run it, a person judges).' Explain why that is not enough, using Group 4's Banking CRM Onboarding Agent and MBairline Feedback Assistant (Week 8 session).
questions.modelAnswer: An approval step alone does not place a task on the Week 7 map. Top-right, 'Agents run it, a person judges', needs two things: no single right answer, and a process that pauses for the person's judgment and then continues with it. The CRM agent fits: the Zap waits at the Human in the Loop step, and Gmail sends only after the manager approves. MBairline also has a manager review, but the agent's report and draft are complete without the person, and the manager 'could also have done this entire process alone', so it sits bottom-right, 'A person decides, AI alongside'. As Group 4 (the Week 8 Zapier-agents team) put it, 'Judgment by a person, or accountability, does not on its own make it top-right', so ask both map questions every time.
questions.explanation: (1) the rule stated — two conditions for top-right; (2) both cases used as a contrast; (3) the rejected reasoning named (accountability or an approval step does not place a task); (4) the advice to ask both map questions.
questions.source: Group 4 Week 8 session, placement reasoning

questions.stem: According to the Week 9 deck, which three parts must a product have before it counts as an agent?
options: A model choosing each step, tools, and a loop that runs to a stop rule
A chat window, a model, and a database that stores every past conversation
A trigger, a schedule and a dashboard of past runs
Memory, MCP connectors and a skill for each task
questions.explanation: 'It needs a model that chooses each next step, tools it uses to look things up or change things, and a loop that reads each result and decides again until a stop rule ends the run… a product without them is a chatbot or an automation.'
questions.trap: 'Memory, MCP connectors and a skill' names Week 8's 'hands' and memory, which are harness settings, not the definition. A trigger and a schedule describe how a run starts, not what makes it an agent.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 4

questions.stem: Week 9 gave three tests for 'agent washing'. A vendor's customer-service 'agent' follows a fixed flowchart, and a model writes the reply text at one step. Which test does it fail, and what is it really?
options: Test 2 (Does it use tools and read the results?); an assistant that writes text
Test 1 (Does a model choose the next step?); 'a workflow with an AI step'
Test 3 (Does it read the result and decide again?); a one-shot automation
None of the three; it is an agent, because a model writes each reply
questions.explanation: Test 1 asks 'Does a model choose the next step?' Here the flowchart chooses every next step and the model only fills in one of them. Prof Roh: products fail 'most often the first: many products sold as agents follow a fixed flowchart'. An agent needs all three parts at once.
questions.trap: 'It is an agent, because a model writes each reply' is the checkpoint distractor: writing text at one step is not choosing the next step.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 8 tests and checkpoint Q2

questions.stem: Week 9 gave six card questions for reading any agent product. Which two draw the territory map?
options: Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q5 (Where does a person approve?)
Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) and Q5 (Where does a person approve?)
Q3 (What can it touch?) and Q6 (Where does it run, and where does your data go?)
Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?)
questions.explanation: The deck: Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?) draw the map, and 'the other questions describe a product once you have placed it'. Across the map: Q1 (Who starts a run?) — you on the left; a schedule, an event or the agent itself on the right. Up the map: Q3 (What can it touch?) — only reads at the bottom, changes things at the top. Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) sets the dot's size, and Q1 (who starts it), Q2 (how long it runs) and Q5 (Where does a person approve?) together describe autonomy.
questions.trap: Q5 (Where does a person approve?) feels as if it should draw the map because gates matter, but it describes the dot after you place it.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 14–15

questions.stem: For Q3 (What can it touch?), the Week 9 deck says to read:
options: The vendor's marketing page and product demo
The system prompt that lists what it may do
'The permissions it holds in its settings, because a prompt can only ask'
The model card published by the model maker
questions.explanation: Q3 (What can it touch?) is read from 'the permissions it holds (hands)'. A prompt is a sentence the model reads; a permission is a setting the harness enforces. This is Week 6's wall again, and the PS7 (one job, seven agent families) lesson 'a setting or a sentence'.
questions.trap: 'The system prompt that lists what it may do' is the prompt-vs-harness swap. Marketing pages and model cards describe intentions, not permissions.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 10

questions.stem: A product reads three news sites every Monday at 8 AM and emails you a summary. It cannot click, buy or edit anything. Which region of the Week 9 territory map is it in?
options: Monitor (it starts without you, it only reads)
Delegate (you start it, it changes things)
Ask (you start it, it only reads)
Autopilot (it starts without you, it changes things)
questions.explanation: Q1 (Who starts a run?): a schedule, so it sits on the right. Q3 (What can it touch?): it only reads and reports, so it sits at the bottom. Right + bottom = Monitor: 'it starts itself and only reads and reports, like a Monday news digest'. Autopilot would need it to change things beyond its reply.
questions.trap: Monitor and Autopilot both start without you; only Autopilot changes things. Emailing the summary to you is its reply, not an action on others.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, checkpoint Q1

questions.stem: Your PS6 (Earnings Watch) watcher pushes briefs to the main branch every day at 6:07 AM. Which region of the territory map is it in, and which single card question would you change to put a person before the action?
options: Monitor; change Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) so a person reads first
Autopilot; change Q5 (Where does a person approve?): push to a branch and open a pull request
Delegate; change Q1 (Who starts a run?) so it only drafts the brief
Autopilot; change Q6 (Where does it run?) to a local machine you can watch
questions.explanation: Q1 (Who starts a run?): a clock, so the right side. Q3 (What can it touch?): it changes your repository by pushing to main, so the top. Right + top = Autopilot (it starts without you, it changes things). To put a person before the action you change Q5 (Where does a person approve?): 'Make it push to a branch and open a pull request, as in Week 8, and a person approves before anything reaches main.' 'One setting moves the gate.'
questions.trap: Q6 (where it runs) tempts because it sounds like governance, but watching the machine is not an approval. Monitor (it starts without you, it only reads) is wrong because pushing to main changes things.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 12 worked example

questions.stem: Prof Roh said two card questions are 'the costliest to find out after launch' if a vendor demo leaves them blank. Which two?
options: Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?)
Q4 (What does it remember?) and Q6 (Where does it run, and where does your data go?)
Q3 (What can it touch?) and Q5 (Where does a person approve?)
Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) and Q4 (What does it remember?)
questions.explanation: 'When a vendor's demo leaves Q3 (What can it touch?) or Q5 (Where does a person approve?) blank, ask for the answer before you sign. In my experience those two are the costliest to find out after launch.' The first is the damage it can do; the second is whether anyone can stop it first.
questions.trap: Q1 (Who starts a run?) and Q3 (What can it touch?) draw the map; Q3 and Q5 (Where does a person approve?) are the costly blanks. They are two different pairs.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 10 'In practice'

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the four exits on the 'when is an agent the wrong tool' flowchart?
options: Do the steps never change? → a fixed workflow
Does a stable API or MCP connector exist? → call it rather than click a screen
Is the data confidential? → run it on your laptop
Is an error rare but costly? → a person decides, AI alongside
questions.explanation: The four exits: fixed workflow (the PS5 (the Zapier agent) Zap), call the API (Week 3's LTA), a person decides with AI alongside, and 'Is the job small and frequent? → a formula or a short script'. All no → 'an agent, with a gate'. 'An agent pays off only when the next step depends on what the last step found.'
questions.trap: 'Is the data confidential? → run it on your laptop' sounds sensible but is not on the slide; confidentiality belongs to Q6 (Where does it run, and where does your data go?). The other three are real exits.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 26

questions.stem: Complete the Week 9 line: 'When the dot moves into Autopilot (it starts without you and changes things), the agent acts on a customer's or citizen's case, so …'
options: …the gate can be removed, since it is trusted
…'the gate moves to before the action'
…the gate moves after the fact, to a weekly review
…a bigger model is needed for that case
questions.explanation: Decision line on the business-uses slide. In Ask (you start it, it only reads) and Monitor (it starts without you, it only reads) the person reads afterwards; once the agent changes things in a real case, a person approves before the action (the PM approves each ticket; finance approves every payment).
questions.trap: 'A bigger model is needed' is the model-size trap. 'The gate moves after the fact' is the Monitor setting, where a person reads afterwards.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 22–23

questions.stem: Claude Duet is open only to US subscribers by waitlist. What should a Singapore manager do?
options: 'Use a family available here, with a gate', e.g. a drafting scheduled task
Drop the idea until it officially launches in Singapore
Use a VPN to reach it, since the waitlist is only a formality for outsiders
Ask the vendor for a personal exception to the waitlist
questions.explanation: 'The vendors' terms tie use to supported countries, so a VPN risks the account, and a scheduled task that drafts for you does much of the job here today.' 'Never route around a restriction with a VPN.'
questions.trap: 'Use a VPN' breaks a rule, and 'drop the idea until it launches' is the passive option. Prof Roh's distractors often come in exactly that pair; the answer is the active move that keeps the rules.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, checkpoint Q3 and slides 27–29

questions.stem: IMDA's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI describes an agent by which two things?
options: Its model size and the amount of training data it learned from
Cost per run and latency of each response
Its action-space (what it can touch) and its autonomy
Accuracy and fairness scores on benchmarks
questions.explanation: 'IMDA launched its Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI on 22 January 2026 and published version 1.5 on 20 May.' It describes an agent by its action-space — what it can touch, our Q3 (What can it touch?) — and its autonomy — our Q1 (Who starts a run?), Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) and Q5 (Where does a person approve?). It is voluntary guidance.
questions.trap: MAS's AI risk management guidelines (7 Oct 2026) are the ones that apply to financial institutions, phasing in over 12–24 months.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 30

questions.stem: Week 9 showed Singtel's customer agent, DBS's credit-memo agents and OCBC's KYC agent (HELIOS). The deck's 'why it matters' line for all three is:
options: AI replaced the customer officers on most cases
'A named person keeps the decision'
The agents run without any gate once trained
All three use the same model from one vendor
questions.explanation: Singtel's Shirley (built on Sierra) handled more than 70,000 cases in six weeks and resolved 73% without an officer; DBS agents draft credit memos for about 1,500 bankers and 'the banker owns the memo'; OCBC's HELIOS does KYC before the RM meets a prospect and 'the manager stays accountable'.
questions.trap: The 73% resolved without an officer tempts 'AI replaced the officers', but the officers still take anything off-script and the banker owns the memo.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 25

questions.stem: The Week 9 rule says you should describe a product's autonomy with:
options: Q1 (Who starts a run?), Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) and Q5 (Where does a person approve?), plus the person's role
Q3 (What can it touch?) and Q6 (Where does it run, and where does your data go?), plus the vendor's own label for it
The model's benchmark score, its maker, and the adjective the vendor puts in the product's name
The number of tools it holds, how often it runs each day, and how many connectors are switched on
questions.explanation: 'Describe autonomy with Q1 (Who starts a run?), Q2 (How long does one run go on its own?) and Q5 (Where does a person approve?), and name the person's role.' Examples: Muse is called 'autonomous' yet asks before it sends an email or buys; Claude scheduled tasks are called 'automation' yet run unwatched.
questions.trap: Read the three questions, not the adjective in the product name. Q3 (What can it touch?) is IMDA's action-space, the other half of the description.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slide 13

pairs.left: Q2 — How long does one run go on its own?
pairs.right: The loop and its stop rule
The permissions it holds (hands)
Memory

questions.explanation: 'A question for each part of the agent you already know.' Q1 (who starts it) and Q3 (what it can touch) draw the map; Q2 (how long it runs) is the dot's size; Q1, Q2 and Q5 (where a person approves) describe autonomy; Q3 and Q5 are the costliest blanks.
questions.trap: Q2 (how long it runs) and Q5 (where a person approves) are the usual swap in 'describe autonomy' questions.
questions.source: Week 9 deck, slides 9–10

questions.stem: Match each product or job to its region on the Week 9 territory map (across: Q1 — Who starts a run?; up: Q3 — What can it touch?).

pairs.right: Ask — you start it; it reads and replies

pairs.left: Claude in Chrome filling a form
pairs.right: Delegate — you start it; it acts in a browser

pairs.left: A Monday news digest emailed to you
pairs.right: Monitor — it starts itself; it only reads and reports
